LESSON: DOMESTIC ANIMALS

Grade: SNE  /  physical-impairment / PP2
Subject: General
Strand: Our Home
Topic 3.3: Domestic Animals
Suggested lessons in curriculum: 10

SECTION 1: INTRODUCTION

This lesson covers Domestic Animals, part of Our Home in SNE  /  physical-impairment / PP2 General.

Key inquiry question: Why do we have animals at home?

You will study the official KICD learning outcomes, classroom activities, values, and competencies for this topic. Use Kenyan examples from your county, school, and community throughout.

SECTION 2: LEARNING OUTCOMES

By the end of this topic, you should be able to:

Refer to the KICD curriculum reference at the end of this lesson for the full list of outcomes.

SECTION 3: KEY CONCEPTS AND EXPLANATION

SECTION 4: LEARNING ACTIVITIES

A. At school

Follow your teacher’s guidance for group work, discussion, and practice on this topic.

B. At home with your parent or guardian

1. Read this lesson on Domestic Animals together.
2. Discuss the key inquiry question and give examples from your area.
3. Write five sentences summarising what you learned.
4. Prepare for the revision quiz at the end of this topic.

SECTION 5: CORE COMPETENCIES, VALUES, AND PCIs

Core Competencies to be developed:
Digital literacy: learner manipulates and interacts with digital devices to watch video clips on domestic animals.

Values:
Love: learner enhances caring skills when feeding domestic animals.

Pertinent and Contemporary Issues:
Animal welfare education: learner enhances environmental awareness as they go for a nature walk to observe domestic animals

Link to other learning area:

Domestic animals relates to learning about creation in Religious Activities.

Suggested Learning Resources:

Video clips, charts, name cards, and pictures and picture cut outs about domestic animals, theme-based multi-purpose

Communication Board, adapted digital devices, songs and poems about domestic animals, universal cuffs with padded pencils,

crayons with grips, paintbrushes with enhanced grip, slant boards, foot-boards for learners using lower extremities, book holders

and page turners, animal moulds, non-chlorofluorocarbon based paints, clay/ papier-mâché or plasticine, positioning/ seating

3.3 Domestic

Animals

(10 lesson
s) By the end of the Sub Strand,

the learner should be able to;


a) name domestic animals at

home,


b) identify domestic animals

found at home,


c) care for the domestic

animals at home,


d) value domestic animals at

home.

• Learners are preferentially

seated/ positioned on devices

with worktops at a suitable

height and guided in purposive

groups or pairs to observe

pictures of domestic animals

found at home. The pictures

should be placed mounted on

cardboards or the textbook be

fastened to book holders for

ease of manipulation using

page turners. For learners with

difficulties in vision, the

pictures should be enlarged,

with brighter colour contrast

and placed on a slant board

Why do we have

animals at home?

51

with an inclination that is

preferable by the learner.

• In purposive groups or pairs,

learners are strategically

positioned or preferentially

seated on positioning/ seating

devices whose worktops/ table

tops are at a suitable height and

guided to manipulate digital

devices to watch video clips on

domestic animals. Learners

with short stature, difficulties in

vision, difficulties in hearing as

well as those on positioning

devices should be seated in

close proximity to the source of

video. The screen light/ glare

should be appropriately

adjusted to suit learners with

difficulties in vision. Learners

with manipulation difficulties

could use any functional part of

the body/ appropriate Assistive

technology such as head/ mouth

pointers to operate the adapted

52

digital devices with physical

support.

• Learners are strategically

positioned or preferentially

seated on positioning/ seating

devices whose worktops/ table

tops are at a suitable height and

guided to model domestic

animals using any functional

part of the body/ appropriate

Assistive technology such as

animal moulds. Learners with

severe manipulation difficulties

could describe the materials

used and the procedure for

modelling as a physical

assistant does the actual

modelling under their

instructions.

• Learners are appropriately

positioned/ preferentially seated

on devices whose worktops/

table tops are at appropriate

height and guided to draw/

trace/ mount cut outs of

domestic animals using any

53

functional part of the body and

appropriate Assistive

technology such as universal

cuffs with padded pencils and

physical support. Learners with

severe manipulation difficulties

and those without limbs could

describe the materials used and

the procedure for drawing as a

physical assistant does the

actual task following the oral

description. The learner is

audio-visually recorded and the

recorded clip saved in the

learner’s e-profile as evidence

of task performance.

• Learners are appropriately

positioned and guided to paint

pictures of domestic animals

using any functional part of the

body, appropriate Assistive

technology, and adapted

painting tools such as

paintbrushes with enhanced

grip with physical support.

Learners with severe

54

manipulation difficulties could

give oral description of the

materials and procedure for

painting. The paint used should

be non-chlorofluorocarbon

based to prevent triggering

allergic reactions among

learners with asthma and

related conditions.

• Learners are guided to trace

images of domestic animals

using any functional part of the

body or appropriate Assistive

technology with physical

support. The image and tracing

paper should be fastened to a

tracing board with sufficient

light. It could also be mounted

on a window pane at an

accessible height and the

sunlight is used to illuminate it

for easy tracing. Learners with

severe manipulation difficulties

could be provided with already

traced picture which they

identify and describe how the

55

tracing is done.

• In purposive pairs or groups,

learners are guided to cut and

paste pictures of domestic

animals using any functional

part of the body/ Assistive

technology for manipulation

and adapted cutting tools with

enhanced grip and physical

support. Learners with poor

fine motor skills could also

mount already prepared

domestic animal picture cut- outs. The chart on which they

paste/ mount the pictures

should mounted on a table top

or worktop for ease of

manipulation by learners with

tremors and spastic muscles.

• Learners are appropriately

positioned/ seated and guided

to colour pictures of animals

using any functional part of the

body, appropriate Assistive

technology, and adapted pencils

or crayons with grips to do the

56

drawing and colouring

colouring with physical

support. They could use slant

boards, and book holders to

perform the task. Learners with

tremors could require splinting

of the most affected limb or use

of hand stabilizers. In severe

cases, learners with

manipulation difficulties could

describe orally the materials,

choice of colour and procedure

for colouring as a physical

assistant does the actual

drawing under their instruction.

• In purposive groups, learners

are guided to take a nature

walk/move outside to observe

domestic animals using

appropriate mobility devices.

Learners should be guided off

rugged/ slippery terrains and

off places with cold, fumes,

heights and dust to prevent

triggering conditions such as

allergic reaction and epileptic

57

seizures among learners who

may have the conditions.

• Learners are preferentially

positioned or seated on their

seating devices in a horse-shoe

formation and guided to engage

in role play about domestic

animals, with roles assigned

according to individual ability

uniqueness. Learners with

difficulties in movement should

be supported to move using

appropriate mobility devices.

• Learners are strategically

positioned or preferentially

seated on positioning/ seating

devices whose worktops/ table

tops are at a suitable height and

guided to match and pair

pictures of domestic animals

using any functional part of the

body or appropriate Assistive

technology with support. The

pictures should be of clear

colour contrast and placed on a

surface or displayed at a place

58

that is accessible by each

learner. For learners with

repetitive body movement

(tremor
s) , the pictures should

be mounted on cardboard or

secured on the table top or slant

board using a preferable

adhesive such as masking tape.

• Learners are strategically

positioned or preferentially

seated on positioning/ seating

devices whose worktops/ table

tops are at a suitable height and

guided to sort and group

pictures of domestic animals

found at home using any

functional part of the body or

appropriate Assistive

technology for manipulation

with physical support. Learners

with manipulation difficulties

could use head/ mouth pointers

to manipulate the pictures.

Learners with repetitive body

movements and those with stiff

muscles could require large

59

pictures mounted on heavy

gauge pieces of paper.

• In purposive pairs/ groups,

learners are guided to feed

domestic animals. Learners on

wheelchairs could move using

mobility devices. Learners with

brittle bone disease should

carry light feedstuffs/

containers while feeding the

animals. Safety precaution

should be taken against injury

from attacks by animals.

• Learners are guided to water

the domestic animals found at

home. Learners with brittle

bone disease should carry light

watering containers to prevent

fractures. Learners could move

using appropriate mobility

devices.

• In purposive groups or pairs,

learners are guided to recite/

mime poems on domestic

animals. Learners with speech

difficulties could alternatively

60

point the words of the poem in

a theme-based multi-purpose

communication board/ chart as

peers recite along.

• Learners are appropriately

positioned and guided to sing/

hum/ dance to the tune of songs

about domestic animals or point

the words in the lyrics of the

song or tap/ clap/ stump

rhythmically as peers sing

along.
